pagetitle: "Named indexes"

# Named indexes

A document can have more than one index — a subject index and an index of
names, say. Declare them in the metadata, in the order they should print:

```yaml
indexes:
  - name: main
    title: Index
  - name: people
    title: Index of Names
```

`name` is what a mark writes to file in that index; `title` is the heading a
reader sees. A name holds ASCII letters, digits, hyphen and underscore and
begins with a letter, because it becomes the id of the section that index
prints under; an entry declaring any other name is reported and declares no
index. A mark says which index it belongs to with `index=`:

```markdown
[Cantor]{.index index="people"}
```

A mark that names no index files in the first declared index. So a document
that declares nothing keeps the single index it has always had, and one that
declares several needs `index=` only on the marks that go somewhere other
than the first.

A placement marker names its index the same way, and each index is placed at
the first marker naming it:

```markdown
::: {.qi-index-here index="people"}
:::
```

A marker that names no index places the first declared one, exactly as a mark
that names none files there. A declared index no marker names goes at the end
of the document, in declared order. A second marker for one index is reported
and places nothing; two markers naming two different indexes are not second
markers for each other.

Every judgement this extension makes about a mark is made inside the index the
mark belongs to. A cross-reference target resolves against the terms of its
own index, a sort key files a term in its own index only, and a range pairs an
opening with a closing of the same index. An opening in one index and a
closing in another are not a pair: each is reported and indexes as an ordinary
locator. A report of one of these judgements names the index it was made in, so
a warning that a target names nothing indexed is telling you nothing in *that*
index carries the term — the term may well be marked elsewhere in the document,
in another index.

**Every index in a PDF.** A LaTeX or PDF render builds every index you
declare, each at its own marker. Two different things build them. The first
declared index is built by Quarto's own PDF loop, which runs the index tool on
the main entry file. Every index after it is built by `imakeidx`, the LaTeX
package this extension loads, which runs the index tool itself — and that run
goes through TeX's restricted shell escape. A stock TeX Live or TinyTeX
permits `makeindex` there, so a normal installation needs nothing from you.
An installation that withholds that permission builds no index after the
first: each of them prints empty, `imakeidx` says so in the LaTeX log, and
this extension neither detects that nor works around it.

`imakeidx` names each index's working files after the index rather than after
the document, so a render leaves `<name>.idx`, `<name>.ilg` and `<name>.ind`
beside your project for every index after the first. Quarto's own cleanup
knows only the main document's files, so these stay behind.

**Mark above the marker, in a named index.** `imakeidx` closes an index's
entry file where that index is printed, so a mark below the placement marker
for its own index reaches no index at all. The extension reports how many such
marks a render found and which block the marker stands in; move the marker
below the last mark filed in that index. The first declared index has no such
limit — its entry file is held open past the place it is printed, so a mark
written below the first marker still reaches the first index, and a mark filed
in the first index is unaffected by where any other index's marker stands.

**Every index in an HTML book.** An HTML book builds every index its chapters
declare and file a mark in, the same as every other format: its chapters are
aggregated through a per-chapter record that carries the index each mark files
in. Each index is placed at the first marker naming it, in whichever chapter
that marker stands;
an index no marker names is printed after them, in declared order, at the end
of the last chapter that places one.

A chapter's stored record outlives the render that wrote it. So a record
naming an index you have since removed from `indexes:` — or renamed — is a
record the book can still read but no longer place: its marks are filed in the
first index the book does declare, and the report names the chapter and the
name, so nothing is dropped and nothing is silent. Render that chapter again,
or the whole book, once the declaration is settled.

`examples/named-indexes.qmd` declares two indexes and writes every one of
those judgements across both — deliberately wrongly, so that a render of it
draws each report in each index; `examples/named-indexes-twin.qmd` is the same
terms in a document that declares none.

```bash
quarto render examples/named-indexes.qmd --to html
quarto render examples/named-indexes.qmd --to latex
```
